query: Which material can be used for to improve the ductility and toughness of the HfZrTi high-entropy alloy (HEAs), and why?

generation.hypothesis: Addition of Nb into the HfZrTi high-entropy alloy will increase ductility and toughness by stabilizing a more ductile BCC phase and enhancing lattice cohesion.
generation.material_initial_state: Near-equiatomic HfZrTi alloy prepared by vacuum arc melting and homogenization.
generation.intervention: Introduce Nb (e.g., 5–10 at%) into the HfZrTi base alloy composition using vacuum arc melting with a homogenizing heat treatment.
generation.conditions: Arc-melt the Hf, Zr, Ti, and Nb feedstock under vacuum, then homogenize at elevated temperature. Perform mechanical testing at ambient conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a predominantly BCC solid solution phase stabilized by Nb.
generation.mechanism: Nb additions reduce the formation of brittle phases and strengthen the lattice through solid-solution hardening, improving ductility and toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Enhanced fracture toughness and greater plastic strain to failure, compared to the Nb-free HfZrTi alloy.
generation.baseline: HfZrTi alloy without Nb, treated under the same conditions for comparison.
generation.boundary: Excessive Nb content could introduce additional phases or increase density, potentially offsetting gains in ductility or toughness.
generation.uncertainty: Exact Nb content for optimal ductility and toughness remains unclear and may require further experimental optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce and compare multiple HfZrTi-Nb alloy samples with varying Nb content via vacuum arc melting and homogenization, then measure structural and mechanical properties.
measurements: Fracture toughness (e.g., CT or three-point bending tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If alloys with added Nb do not demonstrate clearer BCC stabilization and a measurable improvement in ductility or fracture toughness versus undoped HfZrTi, the hypothesis is invalid.

cited_evidence.text:
Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ]. However, most of these RHEAs are generally characterized with high density and poor high temperature oxidation
